Welcome to Vocalis, our Track C project for contrastive speech analytics and temporal flaw grounding. This is footage of the working dashboard, recorded through automated browser actions against the real local backend. We compare a participant with a reference speaking the same text, then ground feedback in measured acoustic evidence. The complete workflow includes audio upload, an editable transcription draft, word alignment, a configurable rubric, synchronized playback, charts and downloadable reports. Recognition and alignment use pretrained models on the CPU. Every report identifies its provider and preserves the rubric used for that evaluation.

Our dataset begins with prominent public speeches by Ronald Reagan and Dwight Eisenhower, with source provenance and matching transcripts. We selected ten complete excerpts and constructed seventy controlled variants. Each excerpt includes near-perfect delivery, mild and severe rushing, slowing, an inserted pause, reduced energy and flattened pitch. The application shows the same text and intended flaws for each paired group. The annotation studio stores exact start and end bounds, severity and the labeling source. Labels come from known transformations rather than the detector itself. We preserve checksums and time mappings, keep an entire source in one split, and hold out Eisenhower by speaker for testing. A separate combined severe example stresses several dimensions together.

Here we demonstrate a real upload and inference workflow using an attributed public LibriSpeech excerpt. The browser sends the WAV to managed storage, then submits an actual local transcription job. The medium recognizer produces an editable draft; the reference text is never supplied as a recognition prompt. A person still reviews the words because names and abbreviations can differ. For this demonstration we confirm the known transcript, select a same-text reference and choose the five-category rubric. The submitted analysis runs real wav two vec C T C alignment and acoustic processing, then persists its result. This identical-audio control should score one hundred. The report includes independent clarity evidence and aligned word timestamps. Local CPU processing needs no paid speech API.

Now we inspect actual stress-test reports. In the monotone example, the participant's pitch variation is deliberately flattened over a known passage. The highlighted interval links to playback, the transcript and the acoustic chart. Its explanation preserves the reference and participant pitch spread, their difference and the detection threshold. Pitch is centered in semitones, while energy is normalized against each recording's speech-active median. This compensates for vocal register and recording gain. The rushing example compares articulation rates over corresponding phrases. The pause example compares adjacent matched word boundaries. These comparisons use participant-aligned time rather than unrelated recording clocks. Selecting a flaw seeks the audio, and selecting a transcript word replays its exact location. The combined severe case demonstrates several interacting deviations rather than a single isolated edit.

Clarity is an additional recognition-based measurement. In this noisy real-source comparison, independently recognized words disagree more with the confirmed transcript than in the reference. The report shows both recognized texts, the word error rates and the additional error rate used for scoring. This is an A S R recoverability proxy, influenced by accents, noise and model behavior; it is not a calibrated human pronunciation diagnosis. Detected regions include mathematical evidence and a specific practice recommendation. The same stored report supports spoken recommendations, browser playback and JSON, CSV and PDF downloads. Historical reports keep their original rubric snapshots. We can edit the rubric for future evaluations without silently changing past results.

Verification separates software correctness from speech accuracy. All seventy controlled variants completed genuine inference. Speaker-held-out testing achieved an F one score of zero point eight and mean matched boundary error of approximately zero point two nine seconds. Four preselected public clips were transcribed three times each through the real API. The larger draft model reduced word error rate from four point eight two percent to three point six one percent, with identical repeats. Sixty-four backend tests, twenty-four frontend tests and seven full browser workflows passed. Those workflows cover real analysis, microphone capture, downloads, annotations, rubric editing and mobile pages. Our six-page technical document explains dataset construction, model architecture, scoring and reproducibility. The contribution is a transparent, replayable comparison, with limitations stated alongside the evidence.
